prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Thousands of people marched in central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in the country after the end of the year. Thousands staged a mass march through Baghdad, Iraq, on Saturday to protest a planned U.S.-Iraq security deal. The political party of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr called for the rally. At one point, several speakers at a podium addressed the mass of people, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal. "End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!" one speaker shouted in English. Hazem al-Araji, a senior al-Sadr aide, told protesters their voices would be heard in America. "Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his 'Black House' -- in which you shouted out, 'No, no, America!'" he said.  Watch protesters wave flags, swarm street » . "This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!" al-Araji exclaimed. Protesters clogged several streets in the capital, waving Iraqi flags and kicking up dust. The demonstration, the largest in Baghdad in several months, was largely peaceful. Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said in Washington on Thursday a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq had "been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators" and was being reviewed by the two governments. A U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq expires December 31, and U.S. officials are examining "contingencies" in case the Iraqi government is unable to sell the status-of-forces deal to the country's various factions, a senior Bush administration official said this week. The same official said negotiations on the pact had finished and the text was final. The official said the "final" draft calls for U.S. troops to be out of Iraqi cities by June 2009 and out of Iraq by the end of 2011 unless the Iraqis ask the United States to stay. The U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said negotiators had also "reached a compromise" on the issue of U.S. troops remaining immune from Iraqi law -- an issue that was a major hurdle in the talks. Baghdad has sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit grave mistakes in the course of their duties. The United States has insisted its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) —** Thousands of people marched through central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in the country beyond the end of the year.

The political party of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr called for the mass rally. At one point, several speakers addressed the crowd from a podium, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal.

“End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!” one speaker shouted in English.

Hazem al-Araji, a senior aide to al-Sadr, told protesters that their voices would be heard in America.

“Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his ‘Black House’ — in which you shouted out, ‘No, no, America!’” he said.

*Watch protesters wave flags and swarm the street »*

“This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!” al-Araji exclaimed.

Protesters clogged several streets in the capital, waving Iraqi flags and kicking up dust. The demonstration—the largest in Baghdad in several months—was largely peaceful.

Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said in Washington on Thursday that a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq had “been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators” and was under review by the two governments.

A U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq expires December 31. U.S. officials are examining “contingencies” in case the Iraqi government is unable to sell the status-of-forces agreement to the country’s various factions, a senior Bush administration official said this week.

The same official said negotiations on the pact had concluded and the text was final. According to the official, the “final” draft calls for U.S. troops to withdraw from Iraqi cities by June 2009 and from Iraq by the end of 2011, unless the Iraqis ask the United States to remain.

The U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said negotiators had also “reached a compromise” on whether U.S. troops would remain immune from Iraqi law—an issue that had been a major hurdle in the talks.

Baghdad has sought the authority to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes unrelated to official military operations, as well as jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit grave mistakes in the course of their duties. The United States has insisted that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law.

CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — Thousands of demonstrators filled central Baghdad on Saturday to oppose a proposed security pact between Iraq and the United States that would allow American forces to remain in the country beyond the end of the year.

The rally was organized by the political movement of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr. During the march, speakers addressed the crowd from a podium and called on Iraq’s government to turn down the agreement. One speaker, using English, demanded an end to the U.S. occupation of Iraq.

Senior al-Sadr aide Hazem al-Araji told participants that their message would reach the United States. He thanked the protesters and said President George Bush would hear the voices of millions rejecting America, referring to the White House as the “Black House.”

Invoking al-Sadr’s message, al-Araji led chants declaring Baghdad free and demanding that the United States leave. He said the message was not reaching the Green Zone and called on everyone inside the heavily secured area to repeat that Baghdad was free and that America should get out.

Crowds packed several streets across the capital, waving Iraqi flags and stirring up dust. The event, Baghdad’s largest demonstration in several months, remained mostly peaceful.

In Washington on Thursday, Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said American and Iraqi negotiators had reached agreement on a draft status-of-forces accord permitting U.S. troops to stay in Iraq. He said both governments were reviewing the document.

The U.N. authorization for the American military presence in Iraq was scheduled to expire on December 31. A senior official in the Bush administration said during the week that U.S. authorities were considering backup options in case the Iraqi government could not win support for the agreement among the country’s different political factions.

According to the same official, negotiations had ended and the wording of the pact was final. The draft required U.S. forces to withdraw from Iraqi cities by June 2009 and leave Iraq entirely by the close of 2011, unless the Iraqi government requested that they remain.

Speaking anonymously because the talks were sensitive, the U.S. official also said negotiators had found a compromise over whether American troops would be protected from prosecution under Iraqi law, one of the principal obstacles in the discussions.

The Iraqi government had sought authority to detain and prosecute Americans accused of offenses unrelated to authorized military activity. Baghdad also wanted legal jurisdiction over troops and contractors responsible for serious errors while performing their duties. The United States, however, had maintained that its military personnel and contractors should continue to be exempt from Iraqi law.

CNN State Department producer Elise Labott contributed to the report.

outputs.L4:
Thousands of Iraqis marched peacefully through central Baghdad in a rally organized by the political movement of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, calling on the government to reject a proposed security agreement that would allow U.S. troops to remain in Iraq beyond the end of the year.

Demonstrators carried Iraqi flags, banners and portraits of al-Sadr as they moved through the capital under heavy security. Many chanted slogans opposing the continued presence of foreign forces and demanded a timetable for a complete American withdrawal. The protest ended without reports of major violence.

The rally was the largest seen in Baghdad in months and underscored the depth of public resistance to the proposed pact. Al-Sadr’s movement, which has consistently opposed the U.S. military presence, argued that the agreement would compromise Iraqi sovereignty and prolong the occupation.

Iraqi and U.S. negotiators had been working for months on the accord, intended to provide a legal framework for American military operations after the existing United Nations mandate expires on December 31. The negotiated draft was being reviewed by the Iraqi government, where it faced objections over withdrawal dates, Iraqi control of military operations and the legal status of U.S. personnel.

Supporters of the agreement said it was necessary to prevent a legal and security vacuum while Iraqi forces continued to assume responsibility for the country’s defense. Opponents maintained that any extension of the U.S. presence should be narrowly limited and subject to firm guarantees of Iraqi authority.

The size of the demonstration increased pressure on the government as it considered whether to approve the draft and submit it to Iraq’s parliament. With the U.N. deadline approaching, officials faced the difficult task of balancing security concerns, relations with Washington and widespread demands for the restoration of full national sovereignty.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about thousands of Muqtada al-Sadr supporters marching in Baghdad to oppose the proposed U.S.-Iraq security agreement extending the American troop presence beyond 2008.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thousands march in Baghdad against proposed U.S.-Iraq security pact**

**BAGHDAD, Iraq** — Thousands of supporters of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr marched through Baghdad on Saturday, protesting a proposed security agreement that would allow U.S. forces to remain in Iraq beyond the end of 2008.

Demonstrators carried Iraqi flags and chanted slogans demanding the withdrawal of American troops. Organizers said the march reflected widespread opposition to any agreement that could undermine Iraq’s sovereignty or prolong the U.S. military presence.

The proposed pact would provide a legal framework for American forces after the United Nations mandate authorizing their presence expires December 31. Iraqi and U.S. negotiators have been working to resolve disagreements over issues including a timetable for withdrawal, Iraqi control over military operations and legal jurisdiction over U.S. personnel.

Al-Sadr, whose movement commands strong support among Baghdad’s Shiite working class, has repeatedly called for U.S. troops to leave Iraq. His followers have warned Iraqi lawmakers not to approve the agreement without firm guarantees that foreign forces will withdraw.

Supporters of the pact argue that Iraq’s security forces still need American assistance despite significant reductions in violence. Critics say the agreement could leave Iraq dependent on Washington and expose U.S. troops and contractors to insufficient Iraqi oversight.

The deal must be approved by Iraq’s political leadership and parliament before taking effect. The debate comes at a sensitive time for Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s government, which is seeking to balance security cooperation with the United States against strong public pressure for full Iraqi sovereignty.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the mass anti-U.S. demonstration in central Baghdad, including protesters’ chants, Hazem al-Araji’s remarks, and details of the draft security pact.
counterfactuals.output:
Tens of thousands of Iraqis, largely supporters of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, marched through central Baghdad to protest the proposed U.S.–Iraqi security agreement. Demonstrators waved Iraqi flags, burned U.S. flags and an effigy of President George W. Bush, and chanted slogans including **“No, no to America,” “No, no to the agreement,”** and **“Yes, yes to Iraq.”**

Hazem al-Araji, a senior Sadrist cleric, told the crowd that the agreement would legitimize the American occupation and compromise Iraqi sovereignty. He said Iraqis would reject any pact permitting U.S. forces to remain and demanded that the issue be put to the Iraqi people rather than decided solely by the government and parliament.

The draft pact—intended to replace the U.N. mandate expiring at the end of 2008—set a timetable for U.S. troops to:

- withdraw from Iraqi cities by **June 30, 2009**;
- leave Iraq entirely by **December 31, 2011**.

It also restricted U.S. military operations by requiring Iraqi coordination or approval, barred Iraq from being used as a base for attacks on neighboring countries, and addressed Iraqi legal jurisdiction over U.S. personnel. Under the draft, American contractors would lose immunity, while Iraqi courts could prosecute U.S. service members for certain serious crimes committed off duty and outside U.S. installations. The agreement still required approval by Iraq’s cabinet and parliament, and its wording remained politically contentious.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a breaking-news article dated during the Bush administration about Iraqi protesters demanding that U.S. forces leave, while explaining the negotiations over troop immunity and withdrawal timelines.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS | October 18, 2008**

# Iraqi Protesters Demand U.S. Withdrawal as Baghdad, Washington Debate Troop Immunity

**BAGHDAD** — Tens of thousands of Iraqis rallied in Baghdad on Saturday to demand the departure of American forces, intensifying pressure on Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki as his government negotiates a security agreement with the Bush administration.

The demonstration, organized by supporters of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, filled streets near eastern Baghdad’s Sadr City. Protesters waved Iraqi flags and carried signs rejecting any pact that would permit U.S. troops to remain in the country without a firm withdrawal commitment.

The rally comes as American and Iraqi officials seek to complete a Status of Forces Agreement before the United Nations mandate authorizing the U.S.-led military presence expires on December 31.

Negotiators have moved toward a timetable under which U.S. combat forces would leave Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009, and all American troops would withdraw from Iraq by the end of 2011. Iraqi officials have pressed for those dates to be binding, while the Bush administration has sought enough flexibility to respond to security conditions and to protect troops carrying out operations.

Legal immunity remains one of the most contentious issues. Washington has insisted that U.S. personnel retain protection from Iraqi prosecution for actions performed in the course of official duty. The emerging compromise would give Iraq jurisdiction over American service members accused of certain serious, premeditated crimes committed off duty and outside U.S. facilities. Joint U.S.-Iraqi procedures would help determine whether an accused service member had been acting in an official capacity.

The proposed agreement would also remove legal immunity previously enjoyed by private American security contractors, placing them under Iraqi law.

Supporters of the accord say it would establish a clear legal basis for the U.S. presence while setting an eventual departure date. Opponents argue that the immunity provisions could undermine Iraqi sovereignty and that the withdrawal schedule leaves American forces in the country too long.

Al-Maliki must win approval from Iraq’s Cabinet and parliament, where the agreement faces resistance from Sadr’s movement and concern among other political blocs. In Washington, President George W. Bush has argued that security gains must be preserved and that any withdrawal should avoid jeopardizing recent reductions in violence.

Saturday’s demonstrators rejected that reasoning, calling instead for a complete and unconditional departure.

*This is a historically framed breaking-news article set during the 2008 U.S.–Iraq negotiations.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the Baghdad rally organized by Muqtada al-Sadr’s political party and describe the status of U.S.-Iraqi negotiations over the post-December 31 military presence.
counterfactuals.output:
Muqtada al-Sadr’s party staged a large, disciplined rally in Baghdad—featuring thousands of supporters, including uniformed members of his movement—to demand that all U.S. troops leave Iraq by December 31. The demonstration was intended as both political pressure and a warning that Sadr’s followers could revive armed resistance if the withdrawal deadline were extended.

Under the existing U.S.-Iraq security agreement, American forces were due to leave by year’s end. Iraqi and U.S. officials were discussing whether a smaller contingent might remain, mainly to train and support Iraqi forces, but no final agreement or formal Iraqi request had been made. Iraqi leaders remained divided, and key issues included the number and mission of any remaining troops and whether they would receive legal immunity.
